title: Sapience
description: Villager AI overhaul. Smarter villagers with personalities, emotions, memory, families, and a whole village that runs itself. 100% offline, no LLM
body:
Vanilla villagers stand around going "hrmm" and shuffle between a workstation and a bed. This mod replaces that behavior with a full mind that runs all the time, busy or idle, watched or not.

A villager senses what's around it, forms an opinion, and decides what to do from its own personality, mood, needs, and memory. Put one in the same situation twice and it does the same thing both times, for the same reasons. You can learn a villager the way you learn a person.

## What kind of AI this is

When people hear "AI" now they picture ChatGPT. A giant model on a company server somewhere, guessing the next word. There is none of that here.

This runs on the older kind, the kind that has driven game characters and chess programs for decades. I wrote the reasoning out by hand, step by step. Each tick a villager checks what's actually happening nearby, weighs its options against what it wants and how it feels, and picks one. No training data. No network connection. Nothing ever leaves your machine.

I went this way on purpose, and honestly I'd choose it again. Hand-written logic can't make things up. A villager only ever acts on what genuinely happened in your world, so when one holds a grudge, you can trace that grudge back to the day you earned it. It reacts instantly, it runs offline, and it behaves the same way every single time. The old approach, and for a game like this, I think the right one.

## They remember you. Specifically you.

Every opinion in the village is about a specific person. Feed a starving villager and that villager remembers you fed it. Hit one and it holds a grudge against you, and the ones who saw it happen tell the ones who didn't. Your reputation is yours alone. On a server, your friend's clean record survives whatever you did to yours.

And the memory runs in both directions. Stay away for a day or more, and a villager who has grown close to you will drop what it's doing when you come back, walk the whole way over, and welcome you home. Build something near a curious villager and it will probably wander over on its next break, look your work up and down, and decide what it thinks. And when a villager turns you down, an apology refused, an invitation declined, it shakes its head no, so you can read the refusal from across the yard before a word lands.

## Their own lives, with or without you

Villagers run their days themselves. They pick work, chop, mine, farm, and build, and they get better at a trade the longer they keep at it. Houses go up with doors, beds, and light inside. On a hillside they dig the floor into the slope the way you would, instead of perching a box on a dirt pillar. At night everyone looks for a bed, the ones without gather at the heart of the village to sleep, and somebody usually plants a torch or two where the dark is dangerous.

They court, marry, and raise children, and a child carries traits from both parents, so a family line stays recognizable down the generations. They fall out too. A feud between two neighbors can simmer for days, and you'll see it in how they stand.

One evening in testing I watched a villager cross the square to a neighbor who had just lost someone, and sit with them for a while. I never wrote that behavior. The pieces were all there, grief and empathy and a free evening, and the brain put them together on its own. That single moment is probably why I'm still building this.

## The village governs itself

Left alone, a settlement organizes. It elects a leader and forms a council. Factions take shape and clash, an old guard against a younger crowd pushing for change, and now and then it boils over into a coup. Most villages settle on a shared faith, hold rituals, and run festivals through the year.

They bury their dead too. The first loss founds a small graveyard at the village edge, and later graves fill in beside it in neat rows, each with a true line about who rests there. Beloved of somebody, usually. Mourners visit.

And after a night the whole village survives, a night that honestly tried to kill them, they gather at the center in the first light. Nobody cheers if somebody died. They know the difference.

## Feelings they keep to themselves

Villagers hold their faces together in company. A miserable one stays composed while you're nearby and lets the real mood out at night, alone. Grief lasts. When a villager dies, the ones who loved it remember its name, mourn for days, and carry that loss through the village.

## Danger

A threat sorts the village in seconds. Brave villagers arm themselves and stand their ground. Timid ones run, and the fear spreads as they go. They step in when a friend is under attack, they back out of fights they can't win, and none of it draws blood on screen, so it's fine for younger players.

## Getting started

Find a village and just watch it for ten minutes. Right click a villager to greet it. Sneak and hand one food to start earning trust. Type `/villager` to read what the nearest one is thinking and working toward. Once a villager trusts you, you can ask it to walk with you. It comes along on its own terms and heads home when it's had enough.

## The questions everyone asks

**Will it lag my server?** The test bench packs 80 villagers into one spot and holds 5.8 milliseconds per tick on average, against the game's 50 millisecond budget. A stress run with 250 villagers stays around 35. Villagers far from any player think in a cheap background mode, so big worlds stay cheap.

**Will they wreck my builds?** No. Villagers only break blocks a real player could see and reach, they never touch built structures, yours or theirs, and miners refill the shafts they abandon.

**Will it break my other mods?** It doesn't touch Points of Interest, workstations, golems, or anything outside villagers. But it does replace villager behavior and the emerald shop economy, so other villager-behavior mods will overlap with it. And it's a beta that writes into your save, so back your world up first. That advice is free and it applies to every mod, including mine.

## Where the mod stands

Already in:

- Personalities, moods, needs, and a memory of what you personally did
- A reputation per player, spread through gossip
- Friendship, romance, marriage, children, and inherited traits
- Villages that build, farm, mine, and repair on their own, with homes that fit the terrain
- Elections, councils, factions, and the occasional coup
- Faiths, rituals, and festivals
- Graveyards with real epitaphs, mourning, and a village that remembers its history
- Composed faces in public, real feelings in private
- Bloodless combat, spreading fear, and villagers defending each other
- The homecoming greeting, the curious look-over, the head shake, the dawn gathering

Still coming:

- Trading you unlock through trust instead of emeralds
- More windows into what a villager is thinking
- Whatever players keep asking for that makes a village feel more alive

## About me and the state of things

It's just me. I build this in my spare time, and I've sunk a lot of days into it. The mod is free and stays free. There's a donation link on the page if you feel like helping, and the mod plays identically whether you do or not.

It's early. You will find bugs, probably some good ones, and I genuinely want to hear about them. Reports steer what I fix first, and updates land often.
